tagline.text: A Baroque Marian shrine in Marikina rooted in the Spanish era

location.label: Location
location.text: Corner of J.P. Rizal Street and V. Gomez Street, Santa Elena, Marikina City

children.text: Marikina Church, formally the Diocesan Shrine and Parish of Our Lady of the Abandoned, is a Spanish-era Baroque church in Santa Elena, Marikina City. Construction on its present site began in the late 17th century, it became a diocesan shrine in 2007, and it is known for the longest Holy Week procession in Metro Manila.

The formal name of Marikina Church is the Diocesan Shrine and Parish of Our Lady of the Abandoned (Nuestra Señora de los Desamparados), and locals simply call it Marikina Church. It stands in the Sta. Elena district of Marikina City, at the corner of J.P. Rizal Street and V. Gomez Street. It belongs to the Diocese of Antipolo, and for residents it is a long-standing center of faith and one of the most symbolic buildings in town. The English Wikipedia describes it as the center of Roman Catholicism in Marikina.

The story is said to begin in 1572, when Augustinian friars built a small church of bamboo and leaves at Chorillo, in what is now Barangka. In 1687 Marikina was placed under the Augustinians, and construction of the present building began on this higher ground; it became an independent parish in 1690. There is a record that it was consecrated in 1791, and it suffered repeatedly from earthquakes, fire, the Philippine–American War and World War II. The upper part of the bell tower fell during the wars. The present appearance is the result of restoration completed by Fr. Silvestre dela Cruz by 1957, followed by a major renovation in 2009–2012. Dates and building periods differ somewhat by source, so treat the numbers as a rough outline.

The church is built of adobe (volcanic stone) in a simple Baroque style, marked by a thick, fortress-like facade and ceiling paintings. The three-storey bell tower has a square base and an octagonal upper section. Inside are a main altar and two side altars, ceiling murals of the Mysteries of the Rosary, Machuca tile flooring, stained glass windows and a pulpit, and the arches and pillars create a three-dimensional optical illusion. Sculptures of Jesus and the apostles, completed in 2012, stand atop the pillars on both sides. It is not as large as the cathedrals of Manila, but it is just the right size to walk into in the middle of town and look around quietly.

The church enshrines a Madonna and Child image, Our Lady of the Abandoned. The first image was burned in 1898 during the war, and the image known today was made anew in 1902. On May 12, 2002, the 100th anniversary of the devotion, a bishop performed an episcopal coronation; Pope Benedict XVI granted a decree of canonical coronation in April 2005, and the coronation took place on October 23 of that year. It was declared a diocesan shrine on August 5, 2007. More recently, according to Wikipedia, the earlier image was returned to its donor in 2024–2025, and a new image modeled on the Valencian image was enthroned on August 5, 2025. It is safest to ask the parish before your visit which image is displayed where. Marikina is a city known for the Marikina River running through it and for its shoe industry, and the church sits in its old center, Santa Elena. Wikipedia notes that old houses such as the Capitan Venciong Cruz House, the Dela Paz House and the Old Chanyungco House remain in Santa Elena. Instead of seeing only the church and leaving, take a look at the old houses in the surrounding lanes to better sense the time this neighborhood has lived through. The church visit itself takes about an hour, but with nearby heritage sites and a meal it becomes a half-day outing. At about 19–21km from central Manila, it is an easy day trip as long as you avoid the traffic.

The thick stone facade, round pediment and three-storey bell tower stand out at a glance. After the upper part collapsed in World War II, the tower was restored with a domed belfry. The outside plaza is a good spot to capture the whole facade in a photo.

blocks.title: Ceiling murals and Machuca tile floor

children.text: Ceiling paintings on the theme of the Mysteries of the Rosary and a patterned tile floor set the mood inside. The arches and pillars also create a three-dimensional optical illusion, so we recommend walking slowly while looking up.

blocks.title: Image of Our Lady of the Abandoned

children.text: A Madonna and Child image that residents lovingly call "Mama Ola". It received an episcopal coronation in 2002 and a canonical coronation approved by the Vatican in 2005. Check on site where the image is enshrined and when you can pay your respects.

blocks.title: Statues of Jesus and the apostles

children.text: Sculptures of Jesus and the apostles, completed in 2012, line the pillars on both sides of the church. It is fun to walk around the outside and look up at them one by one.

blocks.title: Longest Holy Week procession in Metro Manila

children.text: During Holy Week, the procession is known as the longest in Metro Manila, with about 87 floats as of 2023, and its scale is among the largest in the country. The schedule changes every year, so check the parish announcements.
Since 2010 the Marian feast day has been observed on
May 12
. Around this time there are more Masses and events than usual, and the area around the church is lively.

On the same J.P. Rizal Street as the church stands the Kapitan Moy Building (Sentrong Pangkultura ng Marikina). Wikipedia notes that it was declared a national shrine in 1968. Visiting it after the church lets you follow the story of Marikina's Spanish era and its shoe industry.

items.title: 1–2 hour route
items.subtitle: Visiting the church and strolling nearby streets

children.text: Arrive at the plaza in front of the church in Santa Elena and slowly take in the facade and bell tower.
Step inside and look at the ceiling murals, Machuca tiles and stained glass. During Mass, observe quietly from the back.
Walk around the outside of the church and photograph the apostle statues on the pillars and the bell tower.
Walk along J.P. Rizal Street to see nearby heritage sites such as the Kapitan Moy Building, then have a light meal at a restaurant in town.

Masses cluster in the morning and evening, so if you are going mainly to look around, midday without Mass is quieter. Mass times may change, so check the parish's Facebook announcements right before your visit.

items.title: Holy Week procession viewing route
items.subtitle: Watching the procession and an evening visit

children.text: On procession day, head to the area around the church in the afternoon and find a spot along the street. The start time differs each year, so check in advance.
Watch the floats leave the church one by one and continue onto J.P. Rizal Street.
Decide on your transport back in advance, timed to when the procession winds down.
The schedule differs each year and the scale is large, so leave extra time for road closures and crowds.
From central Manila the church is about
away (Wikipedia puts Marikina City about 21km from Manila), and via Quezon Avenue and R7 it is said to take about
1 hour
or so by car, depending on traffic.
At heavily congested times it can take much longer, so check fares and times in advance for ride-hailing taxis such as Grab as well.
Travel times differ by source, so check real-time information on a map app before leaving.
From Quezon City it is said to be about
9.7km
via C-5, around
30 minutes
by car, but this comes from a single source and is not confirmed, so check a map app.
Get off at the LRT-2 Marikina–Pasig or Santolan station and transfer toward the town center by jeepney or tricycle.
Check the exact route and fare from the station to the church locally. Tricycles are the most common way to get around town.
Tricycles and jeepneys run in Marikina, and near the church you can explore on foot.
Walking along J.P. Rizal Street from the church is the easy route.
The dry season, November to May, is the best time to visit Marikina Church. As long as you avoid the strongest midday sun, the outdoor plaza and the area around the church are fine for walking.

During Holy Week (the week before Easter), the longest procession in Metro Manila takes place, but it is extremely crowded. The feast day week of May 12 also brings more Masses and events, so for a quiet visit a weekday midday is best.

rows: The most comfortable time to visit.

Marikina has small and mid-sized hotels and guesthouses, but it is easy to visit as a day trip from Manila, so most travelers return without staying overnight. If you want to stay in Marikina, check the travel time from the town center to the church on a map app.

For meals, local restaurants and snack shops around the church and along J.P. Rizal Street are fine. Marikina is famous for its shoe industry, so it is easy to build a route that also takes in Marikina Shoemaking City.
If you visit during a procession or feast day, temporary stalls and snack shops often multiply around the church. Event scale and dates differ every year, so check this locally as well.
The church is a place of worship. Wear clothes that cover your shoulders and knees, and take off your hat when you go in.
Do not use flash during Mass, and avoid taking photos at the front of the altar.

Mass times are known to be early morning and evening on weekdays and several on Sundays, but they differ slightly by source. Check the latest announcements on the parish's official Facebook page (OLA Marikina).
Roads are congested during Holy Week and feast days, so come by LRT-2 or arrive early.
The Kapitan Moy Building is on the same J.P. Rizal Street, so it pairs well with a visit. Check its opening hours locally.
In March to May, when there is little shade at midday, bring water and a hat.
One source gives the address as 641 J.P. Rizal cor. P. Gomez Sts., while another writes V. Gomez Street. Searching for "Our Lady of the Abandoned Parish" on a map app is the safest way.
The church may restrict entry for Masses and events, and crowds gather during Holy Week and feast days. Check the latest announcements before you go.
Move quietly so as not to disturb worshippers and Mass.
Follow on-site guidance on photography rules for the images and in front of the altar.
Beware of pickpockets where Holy Week crowds are thick, and keep valuables in front of you.
In the rainy season, check news of flooding around the Marikina River.
This entry introduces the shoe industry story of Marikina, where the church stands. Travel time in town depends on traffic, so check it locally.
An old mansion on the same J.P. Rizal Street; according to Wikipedia it was declared a national shrine in 1968 and renamed in 1993. Check the opening hours of the doll museum inside locally.
A shopping and dining district reached by heading toward Quezon City, a good place to stop for a meal after visiting the church.
A pilgrimage city that belongs to the same Diocese of Antipolo, which can be added to a church pilgrimage itinerary.
